## Question 1
The code below shows the function I wrote to mimic the built in R mean() 
function.
``` {r}
meanFunction <- function(vect, dropNA=FALSE){
  
  if (dropNA){
    vect <- vect[!is.na(vect)]
  }
  len <- length(vect)
  sum <- 0
  for (i in 1:len){
    sum <- sum + vect[i]
  }
  meanVal <- sum/len
  return(meanVal)
}
```

### Question 1B
The function can remove NA values by passing "TRUE" to the second arg of the function.
If we add NA values to my vector above let's compare the default results to NA removed.
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}

```
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}

```
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
meanFunction(x, TRUE)
```
Now the R mean function:
``` {r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```
As we can see the function I have written and the R function both return a value of 22.5,
which is expected. 
I expect both of these functions to return the same value, as they both perform the
same mathematical operation of calculating the summation of the vector contents and dividing
by length. Both of these functions will result in an NA if NA not removed as summation will equal "NA".

### Question 1D
Here I will perform a t-test on cholesterol levels (col "CHOL") between men and women (col "SEX"). Here my null hypothesis is that there is no difference between cholesterol levels between men and women within this heart failure data, and my alternative hypothesis is that there is a difference between cholesterol levels between men and women within this heart failure data.
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
sex <- data[,2]
t.test(chol ~ sex, data = data)
```
This t-test showed that there is a difference between cholesteral levels between men and women in this group as the p-value is `r t.test(chol ~ sex, data = data)$p.value`, thus the null hypothesis can be rejected. This test had a t-value of: `r t.test(chol~sex, data=data)$statistic`, and `r t.test(chol~sex, data=data)$parameter` degrees of freedom. 

## Question 2

Loading in the data download function:
``` {r}
GEODataDownload <- function(DS, gpl, gsm, PlateAnnotInfo, GenerateMetaData, Technology, CountsFile = NULL){
  library(DESeq2); library(limma); library(data.table)
  if(Technology == "Array"){
    gset <- getGEO(DS, GSEMatrix = TRUE, getGPL = FALSE)
    if(length(gset) == 1) {
      idx <- 1
    } else {
      idx <- grep(gpl, attr(gset, "names"))
    }
    
    if(length(idx) != 1) {
      stop("Could not uniquely identify the requested GPL platform.")
    }
    
    gset <- gset[[idx]]
    print(gset)
    ex <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(gset)
    Pdat <- as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(gset))
    print(Pdat)
    comp <- gsub(" ", "", gsm)
    comp <- gsub(",", "", comp)
    gsms <- paste0(comp)
    #### Set up raw names ####
    sml <- c()
    for(i in 1:nchar(gsms)){ sml[i] <- substr(gsms,i,i)}
    qx <- as.numeric(quantile(ex, c(0., 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99, 1.0), na.rm=T))
    LogC <- (qx[5] > 100) ||
      (qx[6]-qx[1] > 50 && qx[2] > 0) ||
      (qx[2] > 0 && qx[2] < 1 && qx[4] < 2)
    if(LogC){ ex[which(ex <= 0)] <- NaN
    ex <- log2(ex) }
    print(ex)
    sml <- paste("G", sml, sep="")
    f1 <- as.factor(sml)
    design <- model.matrix(~f1 + 0)
    colnames(design) <- levels(f1)
    fit <- lmFit(ex, design)
    cont.matrix <- makeContrasts(G1-G0, levels = design)
    fit2 <- contrasts.fit(fit, cont.matrix)
    fit2 <- eBayes(fit2, 0.01)
    tT <- topTable(fit2, adjust="fdr", sort.by = "B", number = 25000000000)
    #### subset ####
    tT$ID <- rownames(tT)
    ex2 <- data.table(subset(tT, select=c("ID", "logFC", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val")))
    ex2$ID <- as.character(ex2$ID)
    #### annotate with gene names ####
    plat <- PlateAnnotInfo[GPLID == gpl,][,!"GPLID", with = FALSE]
    if(nrow(plat) == 0){ print(paste("There is no annotation information available for", gpl)) }
    plat$ID <- as.character(plat$ID)
    plat <- plat[!duplicated(plat$ID),]
    ex2 <- merge(plat, ex2, by = "ID")
    ex2$ID <- as.character(ex2$ID)
    exraw <- data.table(ex)
    exraw$ID <- as.character(rownames(ex))
    #### annotate raw data with gene names ####
    ex2 <- merge(ex2, exraw, by = "ID")
    #### Generate Meta Data ####
    #### Add Meta data ####
    return(list(Data = ex2, MetaData = Pdat))
  }
  
  if(Technology == "RNAseq"){
    ACC <- paste("acc=", DS, sep = "")
    file <- paste("file=", DS, "_raw_counts_GRCh38.p13_NCBI.tsv.gz", sep = "")
    comp <- gsub(" ", "", gsm)
    comp <- gsub(",", "", comp)
    gsms <- paste0(comp)
    #### Set up DEG names ####
    urld <- "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?format=file&type=rnaseq_counts"
    path <- paste(urld, ACC, file, sep="&");
    if(is.null(CountsFile)) CountsFile <- path
    cts <- data.table::fread(CountsFile, header=T)
    tbl <- as.matrix(cts, rownames="GeneID")
    exraw <- tbl
    #### Gene annotation from AnnotationHub (GEO GeneIDs are NCBI Entrez IDs) ####
    library(AnnotationHub)
    ah <- AnnotationHub()
    orgdbs <- query(ah, c("OrgDb", "Homo sapiens"))
    orgdb <- orgdbs[[tail(names(orgdbs), 1)]]
    annot <- suppressMessages(AnnotationDbi::select(orgdb, keys = rownames(tbl), keytype = "ENTREZID", columns = c("SYMBOL", "GENENAME")))
    annot <- annot[!duplicated(annot$ENTREZID), ]
    annot <- data.frame(GeneID = as.integer(annot$ENTREZID), Symbol = annot$SYMBOL, Description = annot$GENENAME)
    rownames(annot) <- annot$GeneID
    sml <- strsplit(gsms, split="")[[1]]
    sel <- which(sml != "X")
    sml <- sml[sel]
    tbl <- tbl[ ,sel]
    gs <- factor(sml)
    groups <- make.names(c("Ctrl", "Tx"))
    levels(gs) <- groups
    sample_info <- data.frame(Group = gs, row.names = colnames(tbl))
    keep <- rowSums( tbl >= 10 ) >= min(table(gs))
    tbl <- tbl[keep, ]
    ds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData=tbl, colData=sample_info, design= ~Group)
    ds <- DESeq(ds, test="Wald", sfType="poscount")
    r <- results(ds, contrast=c("Group", groups[2], groups[1]), alpha=0.05, pAdjustMethod ="fdr")
    tT <- r[order(r$padj)[1:length(r$padj)],]
    tT <- merge(as.data.frame(tT), annot, by=0, sort=F)
    tT <- subset(tT, select=c("GeneID","padj","pvalue","lfcSE","stat","log2FoldChange","baseMean","Symbol","Description"))
    #### subset ####
    ex2 <- data.table(subset(tT, select=c("GeneID", "Symbol", "Description", "log2FoldChange", "pvalue", "padj")))
    #### Adjust column names ####
    setnames(ex2, c("GeneID", "Symbol", "Description"), c("ENTREZID", "SYMBOL", "GENENAME"))
    #### Get Raw data ####
    GeneID <- as.integer(rownames(exraw))
    exraw <- as.data.table(exraw)
    #### Update column names ####
    exraw$ENTREZID <- GeneID
    #### merge FC and raw data together ####
    mer <- merge(ex2, exraw, by = "ENTREZID")
    return(mer)
  }
}

significance <- function(padj, foldChange){
  if (padj < 0.05 & abs(foldChange) > 1) {
    return(TRUE)
  } else {
    return(FALSE)
  }
}
```

### Question 2F

``` {r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
savedFile$significance <- mapply(significance, savedFile$padj, savedFile$log2FoldChange)
x <- savedFile$log2FoldChange
y <- -log10(savedFile$padj)
ggplot(savedFile,aes(x=x, y=y, color = savedFile$significance))+geom_point() + labs(x = "Log2 Fold Change", y = "-log10(p-value)", color = "Significance")+geom_vline(xintercept = c(1, -1), linetype = 'dashed') + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = 'dashed')
```
A volcano plot can be enterprited by first examining the xaxis. This axis plots the fold change (in Log2), thus negative values are down expressed and positive ones are up expressed. The fold change being in Log2 indicates that a value of 1 means twice as expressed. 

As for the y-axis of the volcano plot, this represents the statistical significance of the differential expression, this indicates if there is a meaningful difference between expression levels in control vs treatment groups (4, 6).

### Question 2G

``` {r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
df <- apply(savedFile[,c(7:64)], MARGIN = 1, meanFunction)
df <- data.frame(
  gene = savedFile[,2],
  log2FoldChange = savedFile[,4],
  padj = savedFile[,6],

df$significant <- df$padj < 0.05

```
MA Plots have average expression on the x-axis, and thus we can interpret this as what genes are expressed the most across either treatment or control conditions. Note for this graph I used Log10(Average Expression) as some of the genes were so highly expressed that the graph was smushed and not very informative. On the y-axis we show fold change (expressed in log2) and represents if a gene is upregulated (positive) or downregulated (negative). The colouring shows if there is a significant p-value between control and treatment expression (7).

### Question 3C
#### Selecting only treatment groups
The treatment group can be determined by using column metadata to return non-"non-failing" disease states.
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
experiment[,experiment$disease == "dilated cardiomyopathy" | experiment$disease == "ischemic cardiomyopathy"]
```

#### Selecting only statistically significant expressed genes
We can select only statistically significant expressed genes by filtering rowData to inlude only values that have an adjusted p-value less than 0.05.
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}

experiment[rowData(experiment)$padj < 0.05,]
```

#### Combining both filters above
We can combine both filters by saving the result of the first filter to a new SummarizedExperiment object and then performing second filter on new object. This could also be done by parsing the output of filter 1 to filter 2, however I am unsure how to do this in R at the moment. 
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
filtered <- experiment[,experiment$disease == "dilated cardiomyopathy" | experiment$disease == "ischemic cardiomyopathy"]

filtered[rowData(filtered)$padj < 0.05,]
```

## Question 4

### Question 4A
I think that bioconductor objects store data with genes as rows and samples as columns due to the historical component of microarray analysis (the only source I could find for this was Reddit r/Bioinformatics (5)). Statistical learning functions expect a different layout, samples x features, due to the layout being setup properly for mathematical operations to be performed across the columns. If we passed the expression data as is through a machine learning model, the model would be able to produce results, however it would not be the ones we likely desire. The model would be set up to predict which genes are involved in a specific condition, instead of predicting if a condition would arise due to the gene expressions present. Additionally, there would be raw fewer observations if we passed the expression data without transposing it, 58 vs 19xxx for each condition. 

### Question 4B
``` {r}
correlationAnalysis <- function(summarizedExperiment, gene, metadata, colData = FALSE){
  # Filter the summarized experiment based on metadata variable
  if(colData){
    
    metadata <- t(colData(summarizedExperiment)[[metadata]])
  }else{
    metadata <- t(rowData(summarizedExperiment)[[metadata]])
    metadata <- t(metadata)
  }
  #Check the type of data that metadata is
  metadataType <- is.numeric(metadata)
  
  if (metadataType){
  #Collect the expression data for the selected gene
  expressionData <- assay(summarizedExperiment,1)
  expressionData <- as.data.frame(expressionData)
  expressionData$Gene <- rowData(summarizedExperiment)$SYMBOL
  expressionData <- expressionData[,c("Gene", setdiff(names(expressionData), "Gene"))]
  
  index <- match(gene, rowData(summarizedExperiment)$SYMBOL)
  
  expressionData <- expressionData[index,]
  
  if (!colData){
    metadata <- metadata[index,]
  }
  
  expressionData <- expressionData[,-1]
  
  # Check if the dimensions are the same so that they can be tested against one another.
  equal <- identical(dim(expressionData), dim(metadata))
  
  #Transform the objects into numerical vectors for correlation test
  
  expressionData <- as.numeric(expressionData)
  metadata <- as.numeric(metadata)
  
  #Proceed with analysis if the dimensions are the same
  if (equal){
  cor.test(expressionData, metadata)
  } else{
    print("The dimensions are not similar.")
  }
  }
}
```

#### Calling function on colData
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
correlationAnalysis(experiment, "HMGN2", "AGE", colData = TRUE)
```

#### Calling function on rowData
```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, class.source = "fold-show", fig.height=5, fig.width=8, results='show', cache=FALSE}
names(rowData(experiment))
correlationAnalysis(experiment, "HMGN2", "log2FoldChange", colData = FALSE)
```
As we can see in the executed code above, the function does not perform correlation analysis on the rowData since the resulting metadata and expressionData objects are not similar sizes. This makes sense as the rowData, in this case Log2FoldChange, is calculated from the raw exression values. Additionally, the function I wrote handles this by not performing correlation analysis on the incorrect dimension objects.
